What is the essential teaching in '29. What to study and what not to study'?

What to study and what not to study', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Ajaan Suchin Suciṇṇo had received his law degree from Dhammasaat University a long time ago and held the practice of the Dhamma in high regard."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. Can you explain the teaching in the section '29. What to study and what not to study'?

This section teaches: *"Ven. Ajaan Suchin Suciṇṇo had received his law degree from Dhammasaat University a long time ago and held the practice of the Dhamma in high regard. He was a student of Luang Pu Lui for many years and then, after hearing of Luang Pu Dune’s reputation, came to practice with him. Eventually he took ordination. After staying with Luang Pu for a while,..."* The core instruction is to turn investigation inward (*opanayiko*) toward what is already present in body, speech, and mind — not to seek the Dhamma outside or in future states. Whatever theme this section addresses, the method is the same: sustained, patient, non-grasping awareness that allows the truth to reveal itself. As Ajahn Mun taught: when the mind sees clearly, there is no longer any need to go looking.

This text mentions the Dhamma. Can you explain its role in practice?

In this text, Dhamma appears in this context: *"Ajaan Suchin Suciṇṇo had received his law degree from Dhammasaat University a long time ago and held the practice of the Dhamma in high regard."* Understanding the Dhamma — the truth, the teaching, the nature of reality is not merely conceptual — it is meant to be verified directly. The Dhamma is *ehipassiko*: 'come and see for yourself.' Bring the quality described by Dhamma into direct investigation: where is it present in your current experience? When seen clearly, each of these Pāli terms dissolves from abstract concept into living reality.
